"'''Another Day in Paradise'''" is a song written and recorded by the English drummer and singer [[Phil Collins]]. Produced by Collins along with [[Hugh Padgham]], it was released as the first [[Single (music)|single]] from his number-one album ''[[...But Seriously]]'' (1989). As with his song for [[Genesis (band)|Genesis]], "[[Man on the Corner]]", the track addresses the issue of [[homelessness]];<ref name=Dean>{{cite book |title= Rock N' Roll Gold Rush |url= https://archive.org/details/rocknrollgoldrus00dean |url-access= registration |author=Maury Dean |year=2003 |publisher=Algora |isbn=0-87586-207-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/rocknrollgoldrus00dean/page/n75 60]}}</ref> as such, the song was a substantial departure from the [[Dance music|dance]]-[[pop music]] of his previous album, ''[[No Jacket Required]]'' (1985).

Collins sings the song from a third-person perspective, as he observes a man ignoring a homeless woman, and he implores listeners not to turn a blind eye to homelessness because, by drawing a religious allusion, "it's just another day for you and me in paradise". Collins also appeals directly to God by singing: "Oh Lord, is there nothing more anybody can do? Oh Lord, there must be something you can say."

The song was Collins' seventh and final [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] No. 1 single, the last No. 1 single of the 1980s and the first No. 1 single of the 1990s. It was a worldwide success, eventually becoming one of the most successful songs of his solo career. It won Collins and Padgham the [[Grammy Award]] for [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year#Recipients|Record of the Year]] at the [[33rd Annual Grammy Awards#Award winners|1991 awards ceremony]], while it was also nominated for [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year#Recipients|Song of the Year]], [[Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance#Recipients|Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male]] and [[Grammy Award for Best Short Form Music Video#Recipients|Best Music Video, Short Form]]. "Another Day in Paradise" also won an award for [[Brit Award for British Single of the Year#Winners and nominees|British Single]] at the [[1990 Brit Awards#Winners and nominees|1990 Brit Awards]]. Despite the awards gained following its release, the song also generated controversy over its subject matter and has received a largely unfavourable reaction from music critics.

The live performance of the song at the [[33rd Grammy Awards|1991 Grammy Awards]] by Collins and [[David Crosby]], who provided backing vocals on the track, was released on the 1994 album ''Grammy's Greatest Moments Volume I''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B000002IXZ/ |title=Grammy's Greatest Moments, Volume 1: Various Artists |website=Amazon |date=13 May 1994 |access-date=21 November 2011}}</ref> In 2009, Collins' version was listed 86th on ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''{{'}}s Greatest Songs of All Time.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-90.shtml |title=Billboard's Greatest Songs of All Time |magazine=Billboard |access-date=1 May 2009| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090425025152/http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-90.shtml| archive-date= 25 April 2009 | url-status= dead}}</ref> "Another Day in Paradise" has since been covered by several artists, including [[Brandy Norwood|Brandy]] and her brother [[Ray J]], [[Jam Tronik]], [[Axxis]], [[Novecento (group)|Novecento]], [[Brad Arnold]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zq46rZ-9SKM |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/zq46rZ-9SKM |archive-date=21 December 2021 |url-status=live |title=3 Doors Down - Another Day In Paradise (live in Manchester 11.03.12) |via=[[YouTube]] |date=12 March 2012 |access-date=22 September 2021}}{{cbignore}}</ref> and [[Hank Marvin]].

"Another Day in Paradise" is a song written and recorded by the English drummer and singer Phil Collins. Produced by Collins along with Hugh Padgham, it was released as the first single from his number-one album ...But Seriously (1989). As with his song for Genesis, "Man on the Corner", the track addresses the issue of homelessness; as such, the song was a substantial departure from the dance-pop music of his previous album, No Jacket Required (1985).

Collins sings the song from a third-person perspective, as he observes a man ignoring a homeless woman, and he implores listeners not to turn a blind eye to homelessness because, by drawing a religious allusion, "it's just another day for you and me in paradise". Collins also appeals directly to God by singing: "Oh Lord, is there nothing more anybody can do? Oh Lord, there must be something you can say."

The song was Collins' seventh and final Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 single, the last No. 1 single of the 1980s and the first No. 1 single of the 1990s. It was a worldwide success, eventually becoming one of the most successful songs of his solo career. It won Collins and Padgham the Grammy Award for Record of the Year at the 1991 awards ceremony, while it was also nominated for Song of the Year, Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male and Best Music Video, Short Form. "Another Day in Paradise" also won an award for British Single at the 1990 Brit Awards. Despite the awards gained following its release, the song also generated controversy over its subject matter and has received a largely unfavourable reaction from music critics.

The live performance of the song at the 1991 Grammy Awards by Collins and David Crosby, who provided backing vocals on the track, was released on the 1994 album Grammy's Greatest Moments Volume I. In 2009, Collins' version was listed 86th on Billboard{{'}}s Greatest Songs of All Time. "Another Day in Paradise" has since been covered by several artists, including Brandy and her brother Ray J, Jam Tronik, Axxis, Novecento, Brad Arnold and Hank Marvin.

sections.heading: Background
Music video
sections.wikitext: The song's music video was directed by Jim Yukich and produced by Paul Flattery of FYI.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6668700/|title = Phil Collins: Another Day in Paradise (Video 1989) - IMDb|website = [[IMDb]]}}</ref> The video, shot entirely in black and white, features Collins singing in a dark background, interspersed with images of the homeless, the refugees and the poverty of children in the streets. The music video also features many messages about the homeless, to convey the full message of the song. Collins' part was shot in less than an hour in New York.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
{{music ratings|noprose=yes
| rev1      = [[AllMusic]]
| rev1Score = {{Rating|2.5|5}}<ref>{{AllMusic|id=mw0000606790|accessdate=12 November 2025}}</ref>
}}
"Another Day in Paradise" provoked controversy upon release and was widely criticised.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1990-06-08-9002160903-story.html |title=Phil Collins takes issues but not criticism seriously |last=Heim |first=Chris |date=8 June 1990 |website=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Larkin|first=Colin|author-link=Colin Larkin (writer)|date=14 September 2007|title=The Encyclopedia of Popular Music: Concise|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_NNmFiUnSmUC&pg=PA263|publisher=[[Music Sales Group|Omnibus Press]]|page=263|isbn=978-1846098567|access-date=21 August 2014|edition=5th|quote="...the widely criticised 'Another Day in Paradise'."}}</ref> Some critics found the wealthy Collins unqualified to sing about the poor,<ref name="rs1">{{cite magazine|url=http://www.rollingstone.com/music/song-stories/another-day-in-paradise-phil-collins|title=Another Day in Paradise|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|access-date=2 July 2020|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140726192710/http://www.rollingstone.com/music/song-stories/another-day-in-paradise-phil-collins|archive-date=26 July 2014}}</ref> while others accused him of profiteering from homelessness.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/opinion/is-phil-collins-really-such-a-bad-dad-35522658.html|title=Is Phil Collins really such a bad dad?|last=Donaldson|first=Sophie|date=12 March 2017|website=[[Irish Independent]]|access-date=2 July 2020}}</ref> Collins responded, "When I drive down the street, I see the same things everyone else sees. It's a misconception that if you have a lot of money you're somehow out of touch with reality."<ref name="rs1"/>

''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' gave a positive review, calling it a "poignant" track whose "subject matter is complemented nicely by a subdued, ethereal musical context".<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Single reviews|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=4 November 1989|page=79}}</ref> ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' commended Collins' vocals, saying that he "adopted the cool white-soul tones that fellow travelers [[Paul Carrack]] and [[Squeeze (band)|Squeeze]] have so ably championed."<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Gorman |first=Keith |date=4 November 1989 |title=Pure Pop For Now People {{!}} Singles |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1989/CB-1989-11-04.pdf#page=18 |access-date=1 September 2026 |magazine=[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]] |page=18}}</ref> ''[[Music & Media]]'' characterised "Another Day in the Paradise" as a "devilishly catchy semi-ballad" and a "guaranteed hit that will not leave you alone".<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=4 November 1989 |title=Previews {{!}} Singles |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-and-Media/80s/1989/M&M-1989-11-04.pdf#page=13|access-date=1 September 2026 |magazine=[[Music & Media]] |page=24}}</ref>

Singer-songwriter and political activist [[Billy Bragg]] gave a 2000 interview in which he negatively compared Collins to [[the Clash]], stating, "Phil Collins might write a song about the homeless, but if he doesn't have the action to go with it he's just exploiting that for a subject."<ref>{{cite magazine | url= https://ew.com/article/2000/06/30/billy-bragg-clash/ | title= Bragg-ing Rites | magazine=Entertainment Weekly | first=Rob | last=Brunner | date=30 June 2000 | access-date=9 February 2014}}</ref> In 2003, [[Andrew Collins (broadcaster)|Andrew Collins]] described the song as a "bland redress" for the subject of homelessness in the ''[[New Statesman]]''.<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.newstatesman.com/long-reads/2003/02/give-music-a-chance | title= Give music a chance | work=New Statesman | first=Andrew | last=Collins | date=24 February 2003 | accessdate=14 April 2024}}</ref> In 2007, ''[[Blender (magazine)|Blender]]'' remarked that Collins "wrote the worst song ever about homelessness",<ref>{{cite magazine|title=The 40 Worst Lyricists in Rock|url=http://www.blender.com/guide/articles.aspx?ID=2884|magazine=[[Blender (magazine)|Blender]]|volume=November 2007|access-date=2 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011013235/http://www.blender.com/guide/articles.aspx?ID=2884|archive-date=11 October 2007}}</ref> while Caroline Sullivan of ''[[The Guardian]]'' called it "a song that addressed the issue of homelessness with the same insight as [[Sporty Spice]]'s '[[If That Were Me]]'".<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.theguardian.com/music/musicblog/2007/sep/19/iwishidneverheardofphil | title= I wish I'd never heard of Phil Collins ... | work=The Guardian | first=Caroline | last=Sullivan | date=19 September 2007 | access-date=9 February 2014}}</ref> Writing for the [[BBC]] in 2010, David Sheppard described the song's lyrics as "cringe-worthy" and gave it as an example of Collins "painting the bull's-eye on his own forehead" when it came to his negative status with music critics.<ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/music/reviews/m9nv | title= Phil Collins Going Back Review | publisher=BBC | first=David | last=Sheppard | access-date=16 April 2014}}</ref> In 2016, [[Mark Beaumont (journalist)|Mark Beaumont]] of ''[[NME]]'' called it "arguably the corniest multi-millionaire-notices-homelessness-from-gold-plated-limousine ballad ever recorded".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beaumont |first=Mark |author-link=Mark Beaumont (journalist) |date=5 July 2016 |title=Eight Of The All-Time Best-Selling Albums In The UK Have No Redeeming Features Whatsoever |url=https://www.nme.com/blogs/nme-blogs/the-eight-all-time-best-selling-albums-in-the-uk-that-have-no-redeeming-features-whatsoever-6053 |access-date=31 January 2025 |website=[[NME]] |language=en}}</ref>

It was reported that Collins left the UK for Switzerland in 1997, in response to the election of a [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] government;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2007/oct/14/popandrock2 |title=The ten right-wing rockers |last=Bainbridge |first=Luke |date=14 October 2007 |website=The Guardian |access-date=28 October 2020}}</ref><ref name="Hodgkinson">{{cite news |url=https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radio/article/im-too-sensitive-i-dont-like-being-thought-of-as-middle-of-the-road-07c3fkfjp |title=I'm too sensitive. I don't like being thought of as middle of the road |last=Hodgkinson |first=Will |author-link=Will Hodgkinson |date=28 January 2016 |website=The Times |access-date=28 October 2020}}{{Subscription required}}</ref> Collins had actually left previously to be with his future wife Orianne Cevey.<ref>{{cite news | url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/02/28/phil-collins-genesis-to-an-heiress/2d974050-793c-45f5-a88d-5f4610d46b9f/ | title= Phil Collins: Genesis to an Heiress | newspaper=The Washington Post | first=Richard | last=Harrington | date=28 February 1997 | access-date=24 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="Hodgkinson"/> In 2013, [[MSN]]'s Hugh Wilson said this relocation led to further accusations of hypocrisy, since Collins "bemoaned the plight of the homeless in the song 'Another Day in Paradise' " then "lugged his estimated £130 million fortune to Switzerland where the tax regime is far less punishing for the super wealthy".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://him.uk.msn.com/in-the-know/famous-men-and-their-misunderstood-politics-di-canio-fascist-row?page=7 |title=Famous men and their misunderstood politics |work=MSN |first=Hugh |last=Wilson |date=3 April 2013 |access-date=16 April 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222225551/http://him.uk.msn.com/in-the-know/famous-men-and-their-misunderstood-politics-di-canio-fascist-row?page=7 |archive-date=22 February 2014}}</ref>

In a 2016 article for ''The Guardian'', Michael Hann wrote, "Collins has been unfairly criticised for many things, but 'Another Day in Paradise' is not one of them. Criticism of that is manifestly fair." Hann argued that the song patronizes the general public, who "almost certainly encounter poverty more often than [Collins]", and chided Collins for "[equating] his material wealth with his listener's by pointing out that both 'you and me' are in paradise".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/musicblog/2016/oct/14/subjects-songwriters-should-avoid |title=From tax bills to endangered elephants: 10 subjects songwriters should avoid |last=Hann |first=Michael |date=14 October 2016 |website=The Guardian |access-date=18 October 2020}}</ref>

Jamie Wales of ''[[Gigwise]]'' described the track as a "classic", and said of the hypocrisy allegations levelled at Collins, "The truth is Phil collected money for homeless charities from fans who attended his concerts and then donated double the total takings out of his own money."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gigwise.com/features/105706/5-reasons-why-phil-collins-is-actually-a-legend|title=5 reasons why Phil Collins is actually a legend|last=Wales|first=Jamie|date=27 February 2016|website=[[Gigwise]]|access-date=2 July 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cumming |first=Ed |date=2017-01-26 |title=Phil Collins: 'I'm proud of my homeless hit' |url=https://www.standard.co.uk/homelesshelpline/phil-collins-i-m-proud-of-my-homeless-hit-a3450241.html |access-date=2026-09-30 |website=The Standard |language=en}}</ref>

Less<!--not fewer--> than six months after the release of the original Phil Collins version, a cover version by German dance act [[Jam Tronik]] was released as their debut single. In the United Kingdom, the song first charted in March 1990, reaching a peak of number 19 on the [[UK Singles Chart]] in the first week of April. It also charted in Germany and Belgium. Sampled in this version is the drum loop from the 1988 [[Raze (house music group)|Raze]] song "[[Break 4 Love]]". The B-side, "Get on the Raze", also samples "Break 4 Love".

In 2001, siblings [[Brandy Norwood|Brandy]] and [[Ray J]] covered the song for the Phil Collins tribute album ''[[Urban Renewal (tribute album)|Urban Renewal]]''. Produced by Guy Roche and released as the album's [[lead single]] in March 2001, the cover version became a top-10 success in Australia and across Europe, receiving gold certifications in Australia, France, Germany, and Switzerland. In 2002, this version of the song was included on the European edition of Brandy's ''[[Full Moon (Brandy album)|Full Moon]]'' album.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: In their review, ''[[Music Week]]'' felt that the "US siblings are likely to score a hit with this infectiously familiar track."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/2001/Music-Week-2001-05-26.pdf|date=26 May 2001|title=Single Reviews|magazine=[[Music Week]]|page=12|access-date=28 August 2023}}</ref>

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: The music video follows a homeless woman wandering the streets being chastised by various people, including a waitress, a businessman, and a police officer. The video is intercut with scenes of Brandy and Ray J singing on a fire escape and along alleyways, while also following the woman and taking photographs of each incident with a camera. The homeless woman then walks into a luxurious shoe boutique, and the receptionist calls the police to escort her out. When she is dropped back to her makeshift shelter in an alleyway, one of the policemen comes across a series of Polaroids depicting all of the previous characters, including himself, in the homeless woman's place. At the end of the video, Brandy and Ray J come to pick up the homeless woman and walk off with her into the distance.
